children: ) today announced an upcoming poster presentation of Phase 1/2 data on ABCL635 at The Menopause Society’s (TMS) 2026 Annual Meeting, to be held October 20 to 24 at the Hilton Bayfront in San Diego, California.
Details on AbCellera’s poster presentation at TMS are as follows:
Safety, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and preliminary efficacy of ABCL635, an NK3R monoclonal antibody antagonist for the treatment of vasomotor symptoms: a Phase 1/2 study
Thursday, October 22 from 6:15 p.m. to 7:15 p.m. PDT

AbCellera will present safety, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and efficacy data from its Phase 1/2 trial. This includes new safety data from the Phase 1 multiple ascending dose study, as well as new patient-reported outcome data from the Phase 2 study.

ABCL635 is a potential best-in-class investigational antibody drug for the non-hormonal, long-acting treatment of moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms (VMS), commonly known as hot flashes, due to menopause. ABCL635 selectively targets NK3R, a complex transmembrane protein found on hypothalamic KNDy neurons that helps regulate body temperature. ABCL635 is AbCellera’s first program from its GPCR and ion channel platform to advance into the clinic. Additional details are available at www.abcellera.com/pipeline.

The Phase 2 trial of ABCL635 (NCT07118891) is a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in postmenopausal women with moderate-to-severe VMS due to menopause evaluating safety and efficacy of ABCL635.

Hot flashes and night sweats, known as VMS, are the most common menopausal symptoms, impacting up to 80% of women. Many women rate their VMS as moderate to severe, characterized by intense feelings of heat that lead to sweating, chills, and interrupted sleep. VMS are the most frequent reason for seeking medical care for menopause and can persist for over four years after the final menstrual period. VMS have a significant impact on quality of life, are associated with cardiovascular disease risk, and result in lost productivity, career advancement, and income. It is estimated that approximately 12 million women in the US experience moderate-to-severe VMS, of which more than six million seek treatment.
